Conjecture About Arbitrary Even-Order Convexity of ww-Optimization of the Split CIF

Hao Li ††thanks: Namely 李颢 .
Abstract

The ww-optimization problem is a mathematical problem abstracted from a useful tool for general data fusion rooted in various engineering tasks. Purely from the perspective of practical applications for this useful tool namely the split covariance intersection filter (Split CIF), it is sufficient to know that the ww-optimization problem enjoys not only the second-order convexity (namely convexity in conventional sense) but also the fourth-order convexity, thanks to which a guaranteed fast implementation of the Split CIF can be realized. On the other hand, based on certain observations and analysis, the author proposes a conjecture concerning the ww-optimization problem for further mathematical study. The conjecture is that the ww-optimization problem has arbitrary even-order convexity, or in other words, it has the second-order convexity, the fourth-order convexity, the sixth-order convexity, and so on — As mentioned above, whether the ww-optimization problem has higher-order convexity or not might be of little interest itself for practical applications, yet the author believes that the conjecture would stimulate study on systematic mathematical techniques that are potentially interesting and valuable — This paper presents the conjecture in details.

1 Introduction

The split covariance intersection filter (or Split CIF for short) [1] is a useful tool for general data fusion and can be applied in a variety of engineering tasks such as in cooperative intelligent systems [2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8] and in single intelligent system operation [9, 10, 11, 12, 13] as well. An indispensable optimization step involved in the Split CIF, namely ww-optimization (refer to Section 2.1 for details of the problem statement), concerns the performance and implementation efficiency of the Split CIF.

The ww-optimization problem of the Split CIF enjoys the second-order convexity (namely convexity in conventional sense), a proof of which is provided in the author’s works [14, 15]. The ww-optimization problem further enjoys an even more desirable property namely the fourth-order convexity, thanks to which a guaranteed fast implementation of the Split CIF can be realized for practical applications. Relevant details are provided in the author’s another paper [16].

Based on certain observations and analysis, the author proposes a conjecture concerning the ww-optimization problem, namely that the ww-optimization problem has arbitrary even-order convexity, or in other words, it has the second-order convexity, the fourth-order convexity, the sixth-order convexity, and so on.

Purely from the perspective of practical applications for the Split CIF, it is sufficient to know that the ww-optimization problem enjoys not only the second-order convexity but also the fourth-order convexity, and whether the ww-optimization problem has higher-order convexity or not might be of little interest itself. However, the author believes that the conjecture would stimulate study on systematic mathematical techniques that are potentially interesting and valuable. This paper presents the conjecture in details and explain why the conjecture is difficult to handle.

2 Conjecture concerning the ww-optimization problem

2.1 The ww-optimization problem

Matrices mentioned in this paper are symmetric matrices by default. Given matrices 𝐏1​d\mathbf{P}_{1d}, 𝐏1​i\mathbf{P}_{1i}, 𝐏2​d\mathbf{P}_{2d}, and 𝐏2​i\mathbf{P}_{2i} that are positive semi-definite, i.e., 𝐏1​d≥𝟎\mathbf{P}_{1d}\geq\mathbf{0}, 𝐏1​i≥𝟎\mathbf{P}_{1i}\geq\mathbf{0}, 𝐏2​d≥𝟎\mathbf{P}_{2d}\geq\mathbf{0}, 𝐏2​i≥𝟎\mathbf{P}_{2i}\geq\mathbf{0}. Besides, the matrices 𝐏1​d+𝐏1​i\mathbf{P}_{1d}+\mathbf{P}_{1i} and 𝐏2​d+𝐏2​i\mathbf{P}_{2d}+\mathbf{P}_{2i} which normally correspond to covariances of certain estimates are always positive definite, i.e., 𝐏1​d+𝐏1​i>0\mathbf{P}_{1d}+\mathbf{P}_{1i}>0 and 𝐏2​d+𝐏2​i>0\mathbf{P}_{2d}+\mathbf{P}_{2i}>0. For w∈[0,1]w\in[0,1], define

𝐏1​(w)\displaystyle\mathbf{P}_{1}(w) =𝐏1​d/w+𝐏1​i,\displaystyle=\mathbf{P}_{1d}/w+\mathbf{P}_{1i},
𝐏2​(w)\displaystyle\mathbf{P}_{2}(w) =𝐏2​d/(1−w)+𝐏2​i,\displaystyle=\mathbf{P}_{2d}/(1-w)+\mathbf{P}_{2i},
𝐏⁡(w)\displaystyle\mathbf{P}(w) =(𝐏1​(w)−1+𝐏2​(w)−1)−1.\displaystyle=(\mathbf{P}_{1}(w)^{-1}+\mathbf{P}_{2}(w)^{-1})^{-1}. (1)

When w=0w=0 or w=1w=1, 𝐏⁡(w)\mathbf{P}(w) denotes the limit value as w→0w\to 0 or w→1w\to 1 respectively. Then we have

𝐏1​(w)\displaystyle\mathbf{P}_{1}(w) ≥𝐏1​d+𝐏1​i>0,\displaystyle\geq\mathbf{P}_{1d}+\mathbf{P}_{1i}>0, (2a)
𝐏2​(w)\displaystyle\mathbf{P}_{2}(w) ≥𝐏2​d+𝐏2​i>0,\displaystyle\geq\mathbf{P}_{2d}+\mathbf{P}_{2i}>0, (2b)
𝐏⁡(w)\displaystyle\mathbf{P}(w) >0,\displaystyle>0, (2c)

where the third equation (2c) is a natural consequence of (2a) and (2b).

The ww-optimization problem involved in the Split CIF [1] can be formalized as

w=arg⁡min⁡detw∈[0,1]⁡(𝐏⁡(w))w=\arg\min_{w\in[0,1]}\det(\mathbf{P}(w)) (3)

or somehow more desirably as

w=arg⁡minw∈[0,1]​ln​det(𝐏⁡(w)).w=\arg\min_{w\in[0,1]}\ln\det(\mathbf{P}(w)). (4)

The ww-optimization problem can also be formalized as

w=arg⁡minw∈[0,1]​t​r​{𝐏⁡(w)},w=\arg\min_{w\in[0,1]}tr\{\mathbf{P}(w)\}, (5)

where the trace function t​r​{⋅}tr\{\cdot\} is used instead of the determinant function det(⋅)\det(\cdot) — It is worth noting that the determinant and trace functions might be replaced by a generic positive definite real-value matrix function, only if it serves as an appropriate metric (or quasi-metric) that characterizes the “size” of the matrix 𝐏⁡(w)\mathbf{P}(w), yet the two kinds of functions are the popular choices in practical applications 11 1 The author’s another paper [16] explains why the determinant function det(⋅)\det(\cdot) is even preferred over the trace function t​r​{⋅}tr\{\cdot\} for the ww-optimization problem in practical applications, yet for mathematical study, it is still worth taking (5) into account as well..

2.2 The arbitrary even-order convexity conjecture

For a generic function f⁡(x)f(x), if its mm-th-order derivative is always non-negative (or positive semi-definite), namely

dmd​xm​f​(x)≥0,\frac{d^{m}}{dx^{m}}f(x)\geq 0, (6)

then it is said to have the mm-th-order convexity [16]. If f⁡(x)f(x) serves as the objective function of an optimization problem, the author also abuses the expression to say that the optimization problem has the mm-th-order convexity. According to (6), the conventional-sense convexity is right the second-order convexity.

The proposed conjecture is that the ww-optimization problem has arbitrary even-order convexity, more specifically, for k∈{1,2,3,⋯}k\in\{1,2,3,\cdots\} we always have

d2​kd​w2​k​ln​det(𝐏⁡(w))\displaystyle\frac{d^{2k}}{dw^{2k}}\ln\det(\mathbf{P}(w)) ≥0,\displaystyle\geq 0, (7a)
d2​kd​w2​k​t​r​{𝐏⁡(w)}\displaystyle\frac{d^{2k}}{dw^{2k}}tr\{\mathbf{P}(w)\} ≥0,\displaystyle\geq 0, (7b)

where (7a) and (7b) correspond to (4) and (5) respectively.

3 Observations and analysis

3.1 Proof of the conjecture for special cases

The proposed conjecture stems from the ww-optimization problem involved in the Split CIF. As explained in [1], the Split CIF has two special cases naturally. Here is the first special case: If both matrices 𝐏1​d\mathbf{P}_{1d} and 𝐏2​d\mathbf{P}_{2d} are set to zero, then the Split CIF is reduced to the famous Kalman filter [17]. As the assumption that 𝐏1​d+𝐏1​i>0\mathbf{P}_{1d}+\mathbf{P}_{1i}>0 and 𝐏2​d+𝐏2​i>0\mathbf{P}_{2d}+\mathbf{P}_{2i}>0 is always expected, the matrices 𝐏1​i\mathbf{P}_{1i} and 𝐏2​i\mathbf{P}_{2i} in such special case should be positive definite. Then we have a reduced version of (1), i.e.

𝐏1​(w)−1\displaystyle\mathbf{P}_{1}(w)^{-1} =𝐏1​i−1,\displaystyle=\mathbf{P}_{1i}^{-1},
𝐏2​(w)−1\displaystyle\mathbf{P}_{2}(w)^{-1} =𝐏2​i−1,\displaystyle=\mathbf{P}_{2i}^{-1},
𝐏​(w)−1\displaystyle\mathbf{P}(w)^{-1} =𝐏1​i−1+𝐏2​i−1⇔𝐏⁡(w)=(𝐏1​i−1+𝐏2​i−1)−1,\displaystyle=\mathbf{P}_{1i}^{-1}+\mathbf{P}_{2i}^{-1}\iff\mathbf{P}(w)=(\mathbf{P}_{1i}^{-1}+\mathbf{P}_{2i}^{-1})^{-1}, (8)

where the optimization variable ww does not take any effect and the matrix 𝐏⁡(w)\mathbf{P}(w) can be regarded as a constant function in terms of ww. So

dmd​wm​ln​det(𝐏)\displaystyle\frac{d^{m}}{dw^{m}}\ln\det(\mathbf{P}) =0,\displaystyle=0, (9a)
dmd​wm​t​r​{𝐏}\displaystyle\frac{d^{m}}{dw^{m}}tr\{\mathbf{P}\} =0,\displaystyle=0, (9b)

and the conjecture (7) holds trivially for the first special case.

Here is the second special case: If both matrices 𝐏1​i\mathbf{P}_{1i} and 𝐏2​i\mathbf{P}_{2i} are set to zero, then the Split CIF is reduced to the covariance intersection (filter) [18]. As the assumption that 𝐏1​d+𝐏1​i>0\mathbf{P}_{1d}+\mathbf{P}_{1i}>0 and 𝐏2​d+𝐏2​i>0\mathbf{P}_{2d}+\mathbf{P}_{2i}>0 is always expected, the matrices 𝐏1​d\mathbf{P}_{1d} and 𝐏2​d\mathbf{P}_{2d} in such special case should be positive definite. Then we have a reduced version of (1), i.e.

𝐏1​(w)−1\displaystyle\mathbf{P}_{1}(w)^{-1} =𝐏1​d−1​w,\displaystyle=\mathbf{P}_{1d}^{-1}w,
𝐏2​(w)−1\displaystyle\mathbf{P}_{2}(w)^{-1} =𝐏2​d−1​(1−w),\displaystyle=\mathbf{P}_{2d}^{-1}(1-w),
𝐏​(w)−1\displaystyle\mathbf{P}(w)^{-1} =𝐏1​d−1​w+𝐏2​d−1​(1−w)≡𝐀​w+𝐁⇔𝐏⁡(w)=(𝐀​w+𝐁)−1,\displaystyle=\mathbf{P}_{1d}^{-1}w+\mathbf{P}_{2d}^{-1}(1-w)\equiv\mathbf{A}w+\mathbf{B}\iff\mathbf{P}(w)=(\mathbf{A}w+\mathbf{B})^{-1}, (10)

where

𝐀≡𝐏1​d−1−𝐏2​d−1,𝐁≡𝐏2​d−1>0.\displaystyle\mathbf{A}\equiv\mathbf{P}_{1d}^{-1}-\mathbf{P}_{2d}^{-1},\qquad\mathbf{B}\equiv\mathbf{P}_{2d}^{-1}>0.

For denotation conciseness in following derivations, explicit writing of “(w)(w)” for ww-parametrized variables is omitted. Besides, it is taken for granted that all relevant ww-parametrized variables are arbitrary-order differentiable. Furthermore, the following equalities

dd​w​ln​det(𝐌)\displaystyle\frac{d}{dw}\ln\det(\mathbf{M}) =t​r​{𝐌−1​d​𝐌d​w}\displaystyle=tr\{\mathbf{M}^{-1}\frac{d\mathbf{M}}{dw}\} (11a)
d​𝐌−1d​w\displaystyle\frac{d\mathbf{M}^{-1}}{dw} =−𝐌−1​d​𝐌d​w​𝐌−1\displaystyle=-\mathbf{M}^{-1}\frac{d\mathbf{M}}{dw}\mathbf{M}^{-1} (11b)
tr{𝐌1𝐌2⋯𝐌k}\displaystyle tr\{\mathbf{M}_{1}\mathbf{M}_{2}\cdots\mathbf{M}_{k}\} =tr{𝐌2𝐌3⋯𝐌k𝐌1}=⋯=tr{𝐌k𝐌1⋯𝐌k−2𝐌k−1}\displaystyle=tr\{\mathbf{M}_{2}\mathbf{M}_{3}\cdots\mathbf{M}_{k}\mathbf{M}_{1}\}=\cdots=tr\{\mathbf{M}_{k}\mathbf{M}_{1}\cdots\mathbf{M}_{k-2}\mathbf{M}_{k-1}\} (11c)

which correspond to three lemmas used in [16] are also used below. Refer to [16] for details of the lemmas.

Proof of (7a) for the second special case

Substitute (10) into the first two equations of (11) and obtain

dd​w​ln​det(𝐏)\displaystyle\frac{d}{dw}\ln\det(\mathbf{P}) =−dd​wlndet(𝐀w+𝐁)=−tr{(𝐀w+𝐁)−1d⁡(𝐀​w+𝐁)d​w}=−tr{𝐏𝐀},\displaystyle=-\frac{d}{dw}\ln\det(\mathbf{A}w+\mathbf{B})=-tr\{(\mathbf{A}w+\mathbf{B})^{-1}\frac{d(\mathbf{A}w+\mathbf{B})}{dw}\}=-tr\{\mathbf{P}\mathbf{A}\}, (12a)
dd​w​𝐏\displaystyle\frac{d}{dw}\mathbf{P} =dd​w​(𝐀​w+𝐁)−1=−(𝐀​w+𝐁)−1​d⁡(𝐀​w+𝐁)d​w​(𝐀​w+𝐁)−1=−𝐏𝐀𝐏.\displaystyle=\frac{d}{dw}(\mathbf{A}w+\mathbf{B})^{-1}=-(\mathbf{A}w+\mathbf{B})^{-1}\frac{d(\mathbf{A}w+\mathbf{B})}{dw}(\mathbf{A}w+\mathbf{B})^{-1}=-\mathbf{P}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{P}. (12b)

Following (12) and using (11c) namely the cyclic property of trace operation when necessary in following derivation, we have

d2d​w2​ln​det(𝐏)\displaystyle\frac{d^{2}}{dw^{2}}\ln\det(\mathbf{P}) =t​r​{(𝐏𝐀)2},\displaystyle=tr\{(\mathbf{P}\mathbf{A})^{2}\},
d3d​w3​ln​det(𝐏)\displaystyle\frac{d^{3}}{dw^{3}}\ln\det(\mathbf{P}) =−2⋅tr{(𝐏𝐀)3},\displaystyle=-2\cdot tr\{(\mathbf{P}\mathbf{A})^{3}\},
d4d​w4​ln​det(𝐏)\displaystyle\frac{d^{4}}{dw^{4}}\ln\det(\mathbf{P}) =6⋅t​r​{(𝐏𝐀)4},\displaystyle=6\cdot tr\{(\mathbf{P}\mathbf{A})^{4}\},
⋯\displaystyle\cdots ⋯\displaystyle\qquad\cdots
dmd​wm​ln​det(𝐏)\displaystyle\frac{d^{m}}{dw^{m}}\ln\det(\mathbf{P}) =(−1)m​(m−1)!⋅t​r​{(𝐏𝐀)m}.\displaystyle=(-1)^{m}(m-1)!\cdot tr\{(\mathbf{P}\mathbf{A})^{m}\}. (13)

It is not difficult to arrive at the general formalism (13) via mathematical induction and details are saved here. Then set m=2​km=2k and obtain

d2​kd​w2​k​ln​det(𝐏)\displaystyle\frac{d^{2k}}{dw^{2k}}\ln\det(\mathbf{P}) =(2​k−1)!⋅t​r​{(𝐏𝐀)2​k}=(2​k−1)!⋅t​r​{𝐏−1​(𝐏𝐀)2​k​𝐏}\displaystyle=(2k-1)!\cdot tr\{(\mathbf{P}\mathbf{A})^{2k}\}=(2k-1)!\cdot tr\{\sqrt{\mathbf{P}^{-1}}(\mathbf{P}\mathbf{A})^{2k}\sqrt{\mathbf{P}}\}
=(2​k−1)!⋅t​r​{(𝐏​𝐀​𝐏)2​k}≥0.\displaystyle=(2k-1)!\cdot tr\{(\sqrt{\mathbf{P}}\mathbf{A}\sqrt{\mathbf{P}})^{2k}\}\geq 0.

Proof of (7b) for the second special case

Following (12b) and using (11c) when necessary in following derivation as well, we have

dd​w​t​r​{𝐏}\displaystyle\frac{d}{dw}tr\{\mathbf{P}\} =−t​r​{𝐏𝐀𝐏},\displaystyle=-tr\{\mathbf{P}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{P}\},
d2d​w2​t​r​{𝐏}\displaystyle\frac{d^{2}}{dw^{2}}tr\{\mathbf{P}\} =2⋅t​r​{(𝐏𝐀)2​𝐏},\displaystyle=2\cdot tr\{(\mathbf{P}\mathbf{A})^{2}\mathbf{P}\},
d3d​w3​t​r​{𝐏}\displaystyle\frac{d^{3}}{dw^{3}}tr\{\mathbf{P}\} =−6⋅tr{(𝐏𝐀)3𝐏},\displaystyle=-6\cdot tr\{(\mathbf{P}\mathbf{A})^{3}\mathbf{P}\},
d4d​w4​t​r​{𝐏}\displaystyle\frac{d^{4}}{dw^{4}}tr\{\mathbf{P}\} =24⋅t​r​{(𝐏𝐀)4​𝐏},\displaystyle=24\cdot tr\{(\mathbf{P}\mathbf{A})^{4}\mathbf{P}\},
⋯\displaystyle\cdots ⋯\displaystyle\qquad\cdots
dmd​wm​t​r​{𝐏}\displaystyle\frac{d^{m}}{dw^{m}}tr\{\mathbf{P}\} =(−1)m​m!⋅t​r​{(𝐏𝐀)m​𝐏}.\displaystyle=(-1)^{m}m!\cdot tr\{(\mathbf{P}\mathbf{A})^{m}\mathbf{P}\}. (14)

It is not difficult either to arrive at the general formalism (14) via mathematical induction and details are saved here as well. Then set m=2​km=2k and obtain

d2​kd​w2​k​t​r​{𝐏}\displaystyle\frac{d^{2k}}{dw^{2k}}tr\{\mathbf{P}\} =(2​k)!⋅t​r​{(𝐏𝐀)2​k​𝐏}=(2​k)!⋅t​r​{𝐏​(𝐏​𝐀​𝐏)2​k​𝐏}≥0.\displaystyle=(2k)!\cdot tr\{(\mathbf{P}\mathbf{A})^{2k}\mathbf{P}\}=(2k)!\cdot tr\{\sqrt{\mathbf{P}}(\sqrt{\mathbf{P}}\mathbf{A}\sqrt{\mathbf{P}})^{2k}\sqrt{\mathbf{P}}\}\geq 0.

The reason is that (𝐏​𝐀​𝐏)2​k(\sqrt{\mathbf{P}}\mathbf{A}\sqrt{\mathbf{P}})^{2k} is positive semi-definite and hence so is 𝐏​(𝐏​𝐀​𝐏)2​k​𝐏\sqrt{\mathbf{P}}(\sqrt{\mathbf{P}}\mathbf{A}\sqrt{\mathbf{P}})^{2k}\sqrt{\mathbf{P}}.

3.2 Difficulty of the conjecture for the general case

Compared with its reduced version for the special cases presented in Section 3.1, the proposed conjecture becomes essentially different in nature for the general case. For the special cases, the matrix 𝐏​(w)−1\mathbf{P}(w)^{-1}, be it given in (8) or given in (10), is simple as it is linear in terms of ww, thanks to which the explicit and tractable formalisms (9), (13), and (14) of the generic derivatives dmd​wm​ln​det(𝐏)\frac{d^{m}}{dw^{m}}\ln\det(\mathbf{P}) and dmd​wm​t​r​{𝐏}\frac{d^{m}}{dw^{m}}tr\{\mathbf{P}\} can be derived and accordingly the conjecture for the special cases can be directly verified.

However, for the general case, the matrix 𝐏​(w)−1\mathbf{P}(w)^{-1} is much more complicated as it becomes nonlinear in terms of ww. It is at least very hard, if not completely impossible, to derive explicit and tractable formalisms of the generic derivatives dmd​wm​ln​det(𝐏)\frac{d^{m}}{dw^{m}}\ln\det(\mathbf{P}) and dmd​wm​t​r​{𝐏}\frac{d^{m}}{dw^{m}}tr\{\mathbf{P}\} for the general case. By brute-force expansion, the expression of the derivative dmd​wm​ln​det(𝐏)\frac{d^{m}}{dw^{m}}\ln\det(\mathbf{P}) quickly becomes too complicated as mm increases, which can be seen in [16]. The expression of the derivative dmd​wm​t​r​{𝐏}\frac{d^{m}}{dw^{m}}tr\{\mathbf{P}\} also quickly becomes too complicated as mm increases, which can be seen in Appendix A. The author believes that the kind of technique presented by himself in [16] to prove the fourth-order convexity of the ww-optimization problem, which relies on brute-force expansion and ad hoc mathematical skills, is by no means a correct direction to handle the proposed conjecture.

In a word, we need cleverer and systematic mathematical techniques to handle the proposed conjecture.

4 Conclusion

This paper proposes a conjecture concerning the ww-optimization problem of the Split CIF, namely that the ww-optimization problem has arbitrary even-order convexity. The conjecture for two typical special cases can be proved, yet the conjecture for the general case is still waiting for systematic mathematical techniques that are potentially interesting and valuable.
